title: Qutrub's Triplets
intro: Sadid al-Din al-Bahnasi, who died in 685 AH (1286 CE), put into verse the muthallath of Qutrub: words spelt with the same letters whose meaning changes as their first vowel goes from a to i to u. He wrote it in short rajaz stanzas of four half-lines, and says at the start of his own commentary that he composed it “on the letters of the alphabet” so that it would be “easy to memorise”. Most stanzas set the three words inside a lover's complaint against a cold beloved, from the opening “You who are always given to anger” to the close, where he says he wrote the triplets when he saw the beloved's coquetry and neglect. In this recording every triplet stanza is followed by one from a verse commentary by Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Zurayq, which gives the meaning with a, then i, then u, and names its author near the end. The poem was widely copied and commented on; Hajji Khalifa's Kashf al-Zunun reads as if it were Qutrub's own, and al-Zirikli corrects that from its closing lines.

translation: You who are always given to anger,
to leaving me and keeping away:
1.sharh: The poem opens on a lover calling out to a beloved who is forever angry, absent and avoiding him. Al-Bahnasi sets most of Qutrub's word triplets inside this complaint, so the reader learns the vocabulary while following a love story.

translation: love for you has worn me out,
in earnest and in play.
2.sharh: His love has worn him out in every mood, whether the beloved means his coldness or is only playing with him. This first stanza sets the scene; the triplets begin with the next one, each stanza built on a single word read three ways.

translation: My tears are a flood (ghamr),
yet I hold no grudge (ghimr),
3.sharh: His tears overflow, yet for all he suffers he bears his beloved no ill will. Both halves end on the same three letters, and only the first vowel tells the flood from the grudge: this is the game the whole poem plays.

translation: so I said: you greenhorn (ghumr),
leave off your reproaches.
4.sharh: He turns on whoever keeps reproaching him and calls him a greenhorn: someone who has never loved cannot judge a lover. With ghumr the triplet is complete, flood, grudge and greenhorn, in the order a, i, u.

translation: With a: water grown abundant;
with i: rancour kept hidden;
5.sharh: Here Ibn Zurayq's verse commentary begins. After each of al-Bahnasi's stanzas comes one of his in the same metre, naming the meaning of each vowel in turn, so the two can be memorised together: ghamr is water in plenty, ghimr a hidden grudge.

translation: with u: a man who knows nothing
and has never been tried.
6.sharh: Ghumr, the third reading, is a man who knows nothing and has been through nothing. The three meanings come in the order the stanza used them, a, then i, then u; al-Muhallabi supports this one with a line by the poet Abu Dhu'ayb.

translation: He appeared and greeted me with salam,
and stoned my censurer with silam;
7.sharh: The beloved greets the lover and pelts the man who blames him for loving. The same word ends both halves: salam, with a, is the greeting of peace, and silam, with i, the stones thrown at the censurer.

translation: he beckoned to me with his sulam,
his hand stained with henna.
8.sharh: The beloved beckons with his fingers, his hand dyed with henna, a mark of beauty in Arabic love poetry. Sulam are the small bones of the fingers and the back of the hand: greeting, stones and beckoning fingers all from one word.

translation: With a: what the one who greets first says;
with i: hard rock;
9.sharh: Salam is the word said by whoever greets first; silam is solid rock. For the stones al-Muhallabi cites a line of Labid's ode describing a ruined camp, where old writing is kept on the rocks.

translation: with u: a vein in the hand,
a word found in what the Prophet said.
10.sharh: Ibn Zurayq calls sulam a vein of the hand and points to the hadith in which the Prophet says charity is owed for every sulama. The lexicographers explain the word as the small bones and joints, and al-Muhallabi as the bones of the back of the hand.

translation: He enslaved my heart with his words (kalam),
and left wounds (kilam) in my breast,
11.sharh: The beloved's sweet talk has made the lover his slave, and his coldness has left wounds inside him. The words that captured him are the ones that hurt: kalam and kilam differ only in their first vowel.

translation: so I took to the hard ground (kulam)
to win what I wanted.
12.sharh: He crosses hard, stony country in pursuit of the beloved, ready to bear the hardship if it brings him what he wants. Words, wounds, rough ground: the triplet doubles as the story of a lover won, hurt and sent off on a hard road.

translation: With a: speech that is understood;
with i: a wound that hurts;
13.sharh: Kalam is speech whose sense is understood; kilam is a painful wound, the plural of kalm. For the first, al-Muhallabi quotes the Quranic phrase “until he hears the speech of God”.

translation: with u: ground that wears a man out,
it is so very hard.
14.sharh: Kulam is ground so hard that crossing it exhausts and exasperates the traveller. Al-Muhallabi cites a line by Mihyar al-Daylami about a camel that carried him across such ground to the tents of beautiful women.

translation: I came back to a land of black stones (harra),
a land known for burning thirst (hirra),
15.sharh: He finds himself in volcanic country strewn with black stones, notorious for burning thirst: a harsh place to match the harshness of being shunned. The scorched ground and the thirst picture the burning in his heart.

translation: and I said: son of a noble woman (hurra),
pity what has come upon me.
16.sharh: He appeals to the beloved as the son of a free-born, noble mother. Calling a man the son of a noble woman was praise among the Arabs, and the lover hopes good blood will move him to pity.

translation: With a: for stones;
with i: for heat;
17.sharh: Harra names the stony lava ground, hirra the heat, meaning the burning of thirst. Al-Muhallabi illustrates hirra with a line in which a man puts out the fire inside him with jawd, which he explains as a heavy downpour.

translation: with u: for the chosen one
among women kept from view.
18.sharh: Hurra is the free-born woman, the chosen one among women kept secluded at home, as against the slave girl who goes about in public. Al-Muhallabi calls her the woman of pure descent.

translation: Be generous: the hide is rotten through (halm),
and I have no patience left (hilm),
19.sharh: He begs the beloved to be kind, because he is worn out like leather eaten through by worms, and his patience is gone. The spoiled hide is his body; the lost forbearance is his spirit.

translation: and no dream (hulm) has been sweet to me
since you left, my tormentor.
20.sharh: Since the beloved left, even his dreams have lost their sweetness. Body, patience and dreams are all gone: halm, hilm and hulm, rot, forbearance and dream, take everything from him in turn.

translation: With a: a hide holed through;
with i: the forgiveness of cultured men;
21.sharh: Halm is leather holed and spoiled; hilm is the forbearance of cultivated men, who forgive. Al-Muhallabi glosses it as endurance and cites a poet who praises a tribe as lions in war and mountains of patience.

translation: with u: what rises in sleep,
a dream, and mostly lies.
22.sharh: Hulm is what comes to a sleeper, a dream, and Ibn Zurayq adds that most dreams lie. The aside takes a little of the sting from the lover's loss: the dreams he misses were never true.

translation: I gave thanks for Saturday (sabt),
when the man came who shod me in tanned leather (sibt),
23.sharh: He is grateful for the Saturday on which someone brought him sandals of fine tanned leather, ready for a hard journey. Sabt and sibt, the day and the leather, sit side by side.

translation: to walk on the plant called subt
in the hard, trackless waste.
24.sharh: With the new sandals he walks through a waterless wilderness over the plant called subt. Day, sandal and plant, sabt, sibt and subt, make up one short journey.

translation: With a: a day; and when
you give it i, it is footwear;
25.sharh: Sabt is the day of the week; read sibt, it is the leather of a sandal. The sentence runs on from one half to the next, so neither makes sense alone.

translation: with u: a plant, and fodder
for wild cattle when it grows.
26.sharh: Subt is a plant that the grazing herds of wild cattle feed on once it has grown. Al-Muhallabi likens it to marsh mallow.

translation: On a day of scorching heat (saham) he scored
my heart with things like arrows (siham),
27.sharh: On a burning day the beloved's glances cut furrows in the lover's heart like arrows, so the heat outside and the wounds within come together. Glances as arrows are a commonplace of Arabic love poetry.

translation: like the sun shooting its rays (suham)
of light and flame.
28.sharh: The beloved burns him as the midday sun burns, sending out rays and flame. He is a sun in beauty and in cruelty alike. Saham, siham, suham: the heat, the arrows, the sun's rays.

translation: With a: heat grown fierce;
with i: an arrow that is shot;
29.sharh: Saham is heat at its fiercest; siham are arrows loosed from the bow. Al-Muhallabi illustrates saham with a line about a rider whose face is scorched by the endless glare of a mirage.

translation: with u: the light and glow
of the sun as it sets.
30.sharh: Suham, for Ibn Zurayq, is the glow the sun leaves as it goes down; al-Muhallabi makes it the shimmer of the sun's rays in the heat, which looks like threads hanging in the air.

translation: I called on my Lord with a prayer (da'wa)
when he came claiming kin he was not (di'wa),
31.sharh: When the beloved arrives claiming a kinship that is not his, the lover prays. Da'wa is a prayer or call; di'wa a false claim to belong to a family.

translation: and said: I have a feast for you (du'wa)
if you visit me in Rajab.
32.sharh: He then invites the beloved to a meal if he comes to visit in Rajab. Prayer, false claim and invitation share one word, and the lover answers the beloved's pretence with hospitality.

translation: With a: he called on God;
with i: he claimed a descent not his;
33.sharh: Da'wa is calling on God; di'wa is laying claim to a lineage one does not belong to. Al-Muhallabi cites a line taunting a man whose claimed descent is “a false di'wa”.

translation: with u: something cooked
to be eaten in times of joy.
34.sharh: Du'wa is a meal prepared for guests on a happy occasion; al-Muhallabi defines it as whatever people are invited to, food or otherwise.

translation: I made my way to the drinkers (sharb)
and did not guard my share (shirb);
35.sharh: He comes upon a company drinking and lets them take his share of the water without a fight, either out of generosity or because love has left him no will to defend it.

translation: they went off having drunk (shurb)
with no fear of my anger.
36.sharh: They leave having drunk it all, unafraid, since he did nothing to stop them. Sharb, shirb, shurb: the drinkers, the share and the drinking, three words from one root told apart by the vowel.

translation: With a: a gathering of drinkers;
with i: water one drinks;
37.sharh: Sharb is the company of drinkers; shirb is the water a person drinks, his share of it. For the first, al-Muhallabi quotes al-A'sha speaking to his drinking companions when they are already drunk.

translation: with u: the drinking of grape juice
when the grapes are in.
38.sharh: Shurb is the act of drinking, and Ibn Zurayq's example is drinking the juice of grapes in their season. Al-Muhallabi agrees: shurb is drinking itself.

translation: He set out to cross the open waste (kharq)
with the elegant, open-handed youth (khirq);
39.sharh: Someone resolves to cross a vast desert in the company of a gracious, generous young man: a hard road, a fine companion. Kharq and khirq, the desert and the youth, share their letters.

translation: the plainest sign of folly (khurq)
is to ride out into the wastes.
40.sharh: Yet riding out into the empty wastes is plain foolishness. Al-Muhallabi illustrates khurq with Kuthayyir, who calls it folly to ride past his beloved Azza without stopping. Kharq, khirq, khurq: desert, generous youth, folly.

translation: With a: wide country;
with i: a hand that pours out gifts;
41.sharh: Kharq is open country; khirq is a generous man whose hand overflows with gifts. Al-Muhallabi defines khirq as a young man perfect in his good looks; the two meet in the elegant, open-handed youth of the stanza.

translation: with u: a man who has
no manners about him.
42.sharh: Khurq describes the man with no manners or sense about him: folly. Al-Muhallabi gives the same meaning, ignorance and stupidity.

translation: He went far in blame (laha)
after stripping off the bark (liha),
43.sharh: The beloved has heaped blame on him after stripping him bare, as bark is peeled from a branch. The blame comes when the lover has nothing left to shield him, which is why it hurts so much.

translation: and when he saw the beards (luha) go grey
he cut the rope that bound us.
44.sharh: Once the beloved saw grey in the lover's beard, he broke off with him. Arabic love poetry often ties greying hair to being dropped by the beloved: love belongs to the young. Laha, liha, luha: blame, bark, beards.

translation: With a: what censurers say;
with i: a man's stripping of bark;
45.sharh: Laha is the talk of those who blame; liha has to do with a man peeling the bark from wood. Al-Muhallabi glosses laha as quarrelling and disagreement and cites a line by Hassan ibn Thabit.

translation: with u: the hair that grows
on the jaw of young man and grey.
46.sharh: Luha are beards, the hair growing on the jaw of young and old alike. Al-Muhallabi takes it as the plural of the jawbone on which the beard grows; the two explanations come to the same thing.

translation: He dealt with me unjustly (qast)
and did not weigh things justly (qist);
47.sharh: The beloved treats the lover unfairly and gives him no justice. Qast and qist are opposites, injustice and justice, told apart only by their first vowel: one of the neatest pairs in the poem.

translation: in his mouth is the scent of costus (qust)
and of perfumed ambergris.
48.sharh: For all his unfairness, his breath is fragrant as costus and ambergris, so the lover cannot hold the injustice against him. Qast, qist, qust: injustice, justice and a perfume.

translation: With a: injustice in judgement;
with i: justice all accept;
49.sharh: Qast is unjust judgement; qist is the fairness everyone accepts. The Quran uses both: the qasitun are the unjust, and “keep the balance with qist” is a command to weigh fairly (55:9).

translation: with u: a root that tightens
the slackness of the sinews.
50.sharh: Qust is costus root, which Ibn Zurayq describes as a medicine for slack sinews; al-Muhallabi calls it the wood burned as incense and cites a line saying that musk and costus are not the same.

translation: A gazelle, fragrant of scent (arf),
who holds fast to patience (irf),
51.sharh: The beloved is a gazelle with a sweet scent who keeps himself patient. Arf is fragrance and irf patience, and urf, the third reading, follows in the next line.

translation: who bids others do right (urf),
lofty and high in rank.
52.sharh: He also enjoins what is right and stands high in rank. “Holding to” and “bidding what is right” echo the Quran's “Hold to forgiveness and bid what is right” (7:199): the beloved has fragrance, patience and virtue.

translation: With a: a pleasant smell;
with i: patience, which is urged;
53.sharh: Arf is a pleasant smell; irf is patience, the virtue people are urged to. Al-Muhallabi connects arf with the Quranic verse about Paradise “which He has made fragrant for them” (47:6).

translation: with u: words that must be spoken
when doubtful deeds are done.
54.sharh: Urf is speaking up for what is right, a duty whenever people do what they should not. Al-Muhallabi gives the same sense and quotes “bid what is right” (7:199).

translation: I am like a man touched with madness (lamma)
since the hair of my locks (limma) went grey,
55.sharh: Since his flowing hair turned grey he is like a man half mad. The grey of the locks, limma, is what has unsettled him, lamma.

translation: I have no companions (lumma) left,
no wealth left at all.
56.sharh: Grey, friendless and poor: everything has left him at once. Lamma, limma, lumma: madness, locks, companions; the triplet becomes a short complaint against old age.

translation: With a: fear of harm;
with i: the hair of the head;
57.sharh: Lamma, for Ibn Zurayq, is fear of harm; limma is the hair of the head. Al-Muhallabi makes lamma a touch of madness and cites a line about a horse that seems possessed when it charges into battle.

translation: with u: a gathering of people,
old men and boys.
58.sharh: Lumma is a band of people, old and young together. Al-Muhallabi derives it from a word for drawing together.

translation: When it touched my skin (mask)
the scent of musk (misk) spread,
59.sharh: When the beloved's touch reaches his skin, it smells of musk: a single touch perfumes his whole body. Mask and misk, skin and musk, sit side by side.

translation: and from it came what keeps me alive (musk)
and my rest from toil.
60.sharh: That touch is his sustenance and his relief. Mask, misk, musk: skin, musk, and what keeps body and soul together, all from one moment of closeness.

translation: With a: the surface of the skin;
with i: the perfume of India;
61.sharh: Mask is the outer skin; misk is the perfume brought from India. For misk al-Muhallabi quotes the Quran's description of the wine of Paradise, “its seal is musk” (83:26).

translation: with u: what the palm of the man asked for gifts
will not let show.
62.sharh: For Ibn Zurayq musk is meanness, what a man keeps clenched in his palm when asked for a gift. Al-Muhallabi makes it the food and drink that keep a person alive; Ibn Malik's dictionary of triplets also gives meanness.

translation: My tears have filled my lap (hajr),
and my reason (hijr) has worn thin;
63.sharh: He has wept until his lap is full of tears, and love has left him little sense. Hajr and hijr, lap and reason, are filled and emptied together.

translation: were I like the son of Hujr,
I would lose all decorum.
64.sharh: If he loved like Imru' al-Qays, the pre-Islamic poet notorious for his escapades, his good conduct would be gone; so he holds himself back. Hajr, hijr, Hujr: lap, reason, and the name of Imru' al-Qays's father.

translation: With a: the front of the wrap;
with i: human reason;
65.sharh: Hajr is the top and front of the wrap, where a seated man's lap is; hijr is the human mind. Al-Muhallabi adds a legal sense of hajr: a judge's order barring a minor or a spendthrift from managing his own property.

translation: with u: a name that is read
in the lineage of Ibn Hujr of the Arabs.
66.sharh: Hujr is a proper name, known as the name of the father of Imru' al-Qays, the poet of the Arabs; al-Muhallabi says the same. The two lines keep their metre only if the hamza of ism, and of ibn in the second, is pronounced.

translation: He handed me the cool of snow (saqt)
from his mouth, he who is fire's very spark (siqt);
67.sharh: The beloved, who is himself a spark of fire, gives the lover a kiss cool as snow. The fire is the subject of the sentence, so cold and heat meet in one person, a favourite paradox of Arabic love poetry.

translation: and the sparks (suqt) he threw off shone,
flashing like shooting stars.
68.sharh: Then sparks seem to fly from him, flashing like meteors: the gleam of his teeth or his face. Al-Muhallabi reads suqt as sparks, which is the sense here; Ibn Zurayq's gloss in the next stanza makes it a premature child.

translation: With a: snow and hail;
with i: fire from a fire-stick;
69.sharh: Saqt is snow and hail; siqt is fire struck from a fire-stick. Al-Muhallabi agrees about saqt but gives siqt to the child born before its term.

translation: and suqt with u is a child
born before its term.
70.sharh: Suqt, for Ibn Zurayq, is a child born before its time. Al-Muhallabi swaps the last two meanings, and Ibn Malik's dictionary of triplets allows all three vowels in every sense.

translation: He kept me company in a noisy crowd (sarra)
on a night of bitter cold (sirra),
71.sharh: The beloved went with him through a clamouring crowd on a freezing night. Sarra and sirra, the crowd and the cold, share their letters.

translation: and in my purse (surra) not a mustard seed
of gold is left.
72.sharh: He has spent everything on the beloved, down to the last grain of gold in his purse. Sarra, sirra, surra: crowd, cold, purse. The reciter voices the end of all three rhyme words.

translation: With a: a body of visitors;
with i: cold in plenty;
73.sharh: Sarra is a crowd such as a delegation; sirra is bitter cold. Al-Muhallabi quotes the Quranic verse about Abraham's wife coming forward “in a sarra” (51:29), and a line describing a freezing night.

translation: with u: coins tied up
in a fold of one's garment by its fringe.
74.sharh: Surra comes from tying coins into the corner of a garment, knotted with its fringe; money was carried that way, and the knotted bundle is the surra, the purse.

translation: I gave him the pasture's growth (kala') in trust,
with my keeping and my care (kila'),
75.sharh: The lover entrusted the beloved with his pasture, all he had, and gave him his protection, trust and care at once. Kala' and kila', pasture and keeping, are told apart by the vowel; the third reading follows in the next line.

translation: and he gashed my heart and kidneys (kula)
on purpose, with no regard for me.
76.sharh: The beloved betrayed that trust and wounded him deep inside, heart and kidneys, on purpose. Kala', kila', kula: pasture, protection, kidneys.

translation: With a: growth for pasture;
with i: the guarding of loyalty;
77.sharh: Kala' is the growth of the pasture; kila' is watchful care, keeping faith with a friend. Al-Muhallabi quotes the Quran: “Say: who guards you by night and by day?” (21:42).

translation: with u: plural of kidney,
in every living thing born of a father.
78.sharh: Kula are the kidneys, found in every creature that has a father. Al-Muhallabi adds another kula: the patches at the bottom of a large water skin.

translation: Exalted, high of fortune (jadd),
in earnest (jidd) in all he does,
79.sharh: The beloved is noble and fortunate, and everything he does is done in earnest. Jadd and jidd, fortune and earnest, praise birth and character.

translation: I found him at the well (judd)
that lies disused and ruined.
80.sharh: Yet the lover finds him at an abandoned, ruined well, a place where no one drinks; the Quran's “disused well” (22:45) is an image of desolation. Jadd, jidd, judd: fortune, earnest, well.

translation: With a: the father's father;
with i: the opposite of play;
81.sharh: Jadd is the grandfather on the father's side; jidd is earnestness. Al-Muhallabi lists other senses of jadd: majesty, as in “exalted is the majesty of our Lord” (72:3), and luck.

translation: with u: one of the wells
that some Arabs owned.
82.sharh: Judd is a kind of well, of the sort Arab tribes owned; al-Muhallabi too defines it simply as a well, which is the sense of the beloved found at the disused judd.

translation: He sang, and the girls (jawar) sang to him
close by me, in my neighbourhood (jiwar);
83.sharh: The beloved sings and slave girls sing to him, close to where the lover lives. Jawar and jiwar, the girls and the neighbourhood, share their letters.

translation: they listened to the loud cries (juwar)
and swayed away in rapture.
84.sharh: The company listens to the singing at full voice and sways with delight. Juwar, a loud cry, is usually said of people crying out in prayer. Jawar, jiwar, juwar: girls, neighbourhood, loud voices.

translation: With a: plural of girl;
with i: a neighbour to one's house;
85.sharh: Jawar is the plural of jariya, a girl; jiwar is living next door. Al-Muhallabi notes that jawari means both girls and ships, and cites al-Farazdaq for the girls.

translation: with u: the voice of a woman crying
out “woe” and “ruin”.
86.sharh: Juwar is the voice raised by a woman wailing in grief. Al-Muhallabi quotes the Quranic “then they cry out” (23:64), from the same root.

translation: His homes are lived in again (amarat),
and he has lived long (amirat),
87.sharh: His houses are full of people again and he himself has lived to a great age. This is the only stanza whose triplet is a verb, and the vowel that changes is the middle one, not the first.

translation: and his land has flourished (amurat)
after lying in ruins.
88.sharh: His land, once a ruin, is flourishing. House, life and land have all come back to him, and for once the stanza holds no complaint.

translation: With a: someone has made it his home;
with i: he has come into wealth;
89.sharh: Amara is to settle and live in a place; amira, for Ibn Zurayq, is to grow rich. The dictionaries, Lisan al-Arab among them, give amira as living to a great age.

translation: with u: whenever a man has gone deep
into his tried and tested care.
90.sharh: Amura is what happens to land when its owner works it with steady, proven care: it thrives. Al-Muhallabi, too, ties it to bringing land under cultivation.

translation: Tell the doves (hamam)
to weep for me until death (himam).
91.sharh: He asks for the doves to mourn him until he dies. In Arabic poetry the cooing of doves is a lament for lost loves, and he wants their mourning to begin before his death, which love makes certain.

translation: Do you not see, son of Humam,
what sorrows there are in love?
92.sharh: He turns to a man he calls the son of Humam and asks whether he cannot see how much grief love brings. Neither commentator says who is meant; al-Muhallabi only notes that Humam is a man's name.

translation: With a: a bird that coos;
with i: death, as it is decreed;
93.sharh: Hamam is the cooing bird; himam is death, which comes when it is decreed. Al-Muhallabi cites Labid's ode, where a wild cow knows her himam is near unless she drives off the hunting dogs.

translation: with u: someone who is known
by his name, not a nickname.
94.sharh: Humam is a man's given name, not a title or nickname; al-Muhallabi too calls it simply a man's name.

translation: He went in haste among the throng (mala),
and the seas of longing are full (mil'),
95.sharh: The beloved strides off through the crowd, leaving the lover brimming with longing. If mala is read as al-Muhallabi reads it, the open desert, the beloved is setting out on a journey.

translation: and he was dressed in soft sheets of cloth (mula'),
and I said: how wondrous.
96.sharh: The beloved is wrapped in fine, soft cloth, and the lover can only marvel. For mula' al-Muhallabi cites Imru' al-Qays's ode, which compares a herd of wild cows to girls circling a shrine in long-trailing wraps.

translation: With a: a gathering of people;
with i: what fills the seas;
97.sharh: Mala is a gathering of people; mil' is the fill, as in the fill of the seas. Al-Muhallabi separates mala, the open desert, from mala', a gathering, spelt with a hamza.

translation: with u: a fine abqari cloth
set with gold.
98.sharh: Mula' is fine cloth of the abqari kind, worked with gold. The Arabs called anything of rare quality abqari, after Abqar, and the Quran describes the carpets of Paradise with the word (55:76).

translation: He was my like in likeness (shakl);
he enslaved me with his coquetry (shikl),
99.sharh: The beloved is his match in looks and temperament, and has made him a slave with his flirtation. Likeness draws them together; coquetry makes him a captive.

translation: and bound me in hobbles (shukul)
in his love: ah, my ruin.
100.sharh: Then he hobbled him with love as an animal is hobbled, so there is no escape. Shakl, shikl, shukl: likeness, coquetry, hobbles, the whole story of his captivity in one word.

translation: With a: the same as a like;
with i: the charm of coquetry;
101.sharh: Shakl means the same as mithl, a likeness or match; shikl is charming flirtatiousness. Al-Muhallabi cites a line by Umara ibn Aqil about a woman's glances that call out with shikl.

translation: with u: the hobble on a mule,
for fear it might bolt.
102.sharh: Shukl is the hobble put on a mule to keep it from leaping away; al-Muhallabi explains it as the plural of shikal, the rope that ties an animal's legs.

translation: This is the mark of the sandy plain (raqaq);
look at the people of the flats (riqaq):
103.sharh: He points to the signs of a soft, sandy country and tells the listener to look at the people who live on its flats. The stanza is cryptic, built to carry the three words.

translation: after the thin bread (ruqaq), did they speak
the truth, or lies?
104.sharh: He asks whether, once they had eaten his bread, they told the truth or lied, as if testing the loyalty of those who shared his food: among the Arabs, eating together binds people. Raqaq, riqaq, ruqaq: sand, flats, bread.

translation: With a: a stretch of unbroken sand;
with i: bread that is eaten;
105.sharh: Raqaq is a continuous stretch of sand; Ibn Zurayq gives riqaq, with i, as bread. Al-Muhallabi agrees about raqaq and cites a line on riding camels crossing soft sand that crumbles under their feet.

translation: with u: land set apart
under the safeguard of boundary stones.
106.sharh: Ruqaq, he says, is a piece of land marked off by boundary stones. Al-Muhallabi and Ibn Malik give the bread to ruqaq and the drained flats to riqaq, so Ibn Zurayq seems to have swapped the two.

translation: I found him like a lion's mouthful (qamma)
on a mountain with a high peak (qimma),
107.sharh: He finds his companion on a mountain top, helpless as prey in a lion's jaws: in the highest place and the lowest state. Al-Muhallabi cites a line, which he gives to Abu Dawud, in which enemies become a mouthful for the tribe's lions.

translation: cast aside like sweepings (qumma);
I said to him: keep to my way.
108.sharh: He lies discarded like rubbish swept out of a house, and the speaker tells him to follow his own way of life instead. Qamma, qimma, qumma: a lion's mouthful, a peak, sweepings.

translation: With a: the seizing of people;
with i: the top of the head;
109.sharh: Qamma is the seizing of people, prey taken as a lion takes it in its jaws, which is al-Muhallabi's gloss too (it may also mean taking everything at once); qimma is the crown of the head. Al-Muhallabi cites Dhu al-Rumma, who sees the Pleiades overhead like a water bird hovering above his crown.

translation: with u: for sweepings
from a ruined place.
110.sharh: Qumma, he says, is what is tipped out of a derelict house: rubbish. Al-Muhallabi defines it as sweepings, and Ibn Malik notes that it is another form of qumama, refuse.

translation: Do not lean on the clang of iron (sall),
and do not trust the viper (sill);
111.sharh: Advice: do not put your faith in the clash of weapons, and do not trust a snake. The stanza is a string of warnings: war, hidden enemies, spoiled food.

translation: beware of tainted food (sull),
and rise as the man sitting wrapped rises.
112.sharh: Avoid food that has gone off, and get up and go, as a man sitting with his knees bound in his cloak gets up. That way of sitting, the ihtiba', was how Arabs sat in company.

translation: The sound of iron when it rings;
a snake, if given i;
113.sharh: Here Ibn Zurayq breaks his pattern: sall is the ringing of iron, and with i it is a snake. Al-Muhallabi gives the ringing of iron to sull instead, citing Imru' al-Qays.

translation: and water, when it has gone off,
is, with u, not fit to drink.
114.sharh: Sull is water that has turned and cannot be drunk. Only here does the commentary not open with “with a”, holding the vowel back to the end; al-Muhallabi gives the spoiling of meat and food to sall.

translation: He unveils the eyes of a fawn (tala)
and a cheek like wine (tila),
115.sharh: The beloved shows eyes like a young gazelle's, wide and dark, and a cheek flushed the colour of wine.

translation: and his neck among necks (tula)
is soft and supple, never veiled.
116.sharh: His neck is the finest of necks, long and supple, and he does not hide it. Tala, tila, tula: fawn, wine, necks, three stock images of beauty.

translation: With a: young gazelles;
with i: wine that is drunk;
117.sharh: Tala are the young of gazelles; tila is wine. Al-Muhallabi defines tila as thick, boiled wine and quotes a line of verse that begins “it is wine, which goes by the name of tila”.

translation: with u: a neck for whose beauty
the gazelle's neck is the likeness.
118.sharh: Tula is the neck, the kind whose beauty is compared to a gazelle's; al-Muhallabi explains it as the plural of tulya, neck.

translation: I came to him when he was a castaway (laqa),
and he beamed at me when we met (liqa'),
119.sharh: The lover found the beloved neglected and cast aside, yet he lit up when they met: the forgotten are glad of a visitor. This is the first of seven stanzas that al-Muhallabi's own text does not have.

translation: and said: feed me luqa,
that is all I could wish for.
120.sharh: He asked to be fed a sweet of honey boiled thick, the most he could want. Laqa, liqa', luqa: a castaway, a meeting, a honey sweet.

translation: With a: the sweepings of a house;
with i: for war, say it;
121.sharh: Laqa is what is swept out of a house; liqa', with i, is the meeting of enemies in battle, a common sense of the word in classical Arabic.

translation: with u: honey water
you have thickened over the flame.
122.sharh: Luqa is honey syrup boiled over the fire until it sets. That is Ibn Zurayq's gloss; Ibn Malik makes luqa simply the verbal noun of meeting.

translation: He kept me company, a young gazelle (rasha'),
as close as the bucket to its rope (risha');
123.sharh: The beloved, graceful as a young gazelle, stays as close to him as a bucket to its well rope, going down and coming up together.

translation: far be it from him to take bribes (rusha)
in judging, or to fall under suspicion.
124.sharh: He clears the beloved of ever taking a bribe or doing anything suspect; the beloved here seems to be a man who sits in judgement. Rasha', risha', rusha: gazelle, rope, bribes.

translation: With a: for the gazelle;
with i: for ropes;
125.sharh: Rasha' is the young gazelle; risha' is rope, the long rope of a well. Both lose their final hamza here for the metre.

translation: with u: money paid
to the greedy judge.
126.sharh: Rusha is money handed to a judge greedy for it; the word Ibn Zurayq uses for greedy likens him to a ravenous dog.

translation: His saliva is like cloves (zajaj),
and his glance like spear points (zijaj),
127.sharh: The beloved's mouth tastes of cloves and his glances pierce like spear points: sweetness and danger together. A fragrant mouth and glances that wound are both stock images of Arabic love poetry.

translation: and his heart is like glass (zujaj),
a valley swift to ruin.
128.sharh: His heart is as fragile as glass, a place soon laid waste, so his affection cannot be relied on. Sweet mouth, wounding glance, brittle heart: the last half is obscure, but the point is glass that shatters at a touch. Zajaj, zijaj, zujaj: cloves, spear points, glass.

translation: With a: for cloves;
with i: the thrusting of spears;
129.sharh: Zajaj, he says, is cloves; zijaj he ties to the thrusting of spears, though the dictionaries make zijaj the iron spikes at the butt of a spear, plural of zujj. Al-Muhallabi's text does not have this stanza, so there is no second gloss to compare.

translation: with u: the glass that takes much work,
like the glass of Aleppo.
130.sharh: Zujaj is worked glass, the labour-intensive kind, such as the glass of Aleppo. Ibn Malik allows all three vowels for glass.

translation: Better the bite of a thousand snakes (manna)
than to bear a favour thrown in my face (minna);
131.sharh: He would rather be bitten by a thousand snakes than put up with someone reminding him of a kindness done. Throwing a favour in someone's face was a vice among the Arabs, and the Quran warns that it voids charity (2:264).

translation: whoever has the strength (munna)
should find his rest in flight.
132.sharh: Anyone strong enough should escape such favours and be at peace: better far from the giver than under his favour. Manna, minna, munna: snake, favour, strength.

translation: With a: for the snake;
with i: for a gift;
133.sharh: Manna is the snake; minna is a gift held over the one who receives it. Ibn Malik does not give the snake; for him manna is a single act of bestowing or reproaching.

translation: with u: for strength,
the token of mastery.
134.sharh: Munna is strength, the sign of the one who prevails. Ibn Malik notes that munna can also mean weakness, one of the Arabic words that carry their own opposite.

translation: My heart was struck a deep head-wound (amma)
when my good fortune (imma) left me,
135.sharh: When his comfortable life came to an end, his heart took a wound as deep as a blow that reaches the membrane of the brain, one of the gravest head wounds.

translation: so listen, people (umma),
by your Lord, to what has come upon me.
136.sharh: He calls on everyone to hear what has happened to him. Amma, imma, umma: a head wound, good fortune, a people, moving from injury to loss to an appeal.

translation: With a: a gash to the head;
with i: the opposite of hardship;
137.sharh: Amma is a wound to the head; imma is the opposite of distress, that is, plenty and ease. Al-Muhallabi glosses imma as wealth and cites a line by Hatim al-Ta'i.

translation: with u: a body of people,
Arab or not.
138.sharh: Umma is a people, whether Arabs or others. Al-Muhallabi lists three senses of umma, one of them a span of time.

translation: The weakness in my back (qara) came to me
from the business of hospitality (qira),
139.sharh: He complains of a weakness in his back brought on by the business of hospitality. The lines are obscure; the likeliest sense is that the burden of feeding guests has worn him down.

translation: and that, away from the towns (qura):
how would it be among the Arabs?
140.sharh: If hospitality wears him out away from the towns, he wonders how it would be among the desert Arabs, famous for their generosity. Qara, qira, qura: back, hospitality, towns.

translation: With a: the back of a hollow;
with i: food for visitors;
141.sharh: Qara is the back, which Ibn Zurayq puts as the back of a hollow in the ground; qira is the food given to visiting guests, the hospitality the Arabs prized above most virtues.

translation: with u: the plural for towns,
like Mecca or Yathrib.
142.sharh: Qura is the plural for towns, such as Mecca and Medina, the best known towns of Arabia; the Quran calls Mecca “the mother of towns”, umm al-qura (6:92).

translation: Who will give me a sip of those gleaming teeth (zalm),
or the hunting of the ostrich (zilm)?
143.sharh: He longs to taste the beloved's bright mouth, or to catch him as one hunts a skittish ostrich: sweet to the lips, hard to catch.

translation: There is no injustice (zulm) in him,
no word of a lie.
144.sharh: The beloved is free of injustice and falsehood, so the stanza ends on his character after his beauty and his shyness. Zalm, zilm, zulm: the sheen of teeth, the ostrich, injustice.

translation: With a: the water of the teeth;
the second is for ostriches;
145.sharh: Zalm is the moisture of the teeth; the second vowel, i, gives the word for the ostrich. Ibn Malik gives zalm as both snow and the sheen of the teeth.

translation: and zulm, injustice, in a man
is what draws down anger.
146.sharh: Zulm is human injustice, which brings anger on the one who does it. Instead of saying “with u”, Ibn Zurayq simply says the word itself.

translation: Rain (qatr) is the bounty of his hand,
and molten brass (qitr) the flood of death he brings;
147.sharh: His generosity falls like rain, and on his enemies his might pours like molten metal: rain to his friends, ruin to his foes.

translation: aloeswood (qutr) is the breath of his nose,
and his cheek is gold.
148.sharh: His breath smells of aloeswood and his cheek gleams like gold. Qatr, qitr, qutr: rain, molten brass, aloeswood.

translation: With a: rain poured down;
with i: brass that is melted;
149.sharh: Qatr is pouring rain; qitr is brass melted down, the molten metal Dhu al-Qarnayn pours over his wall in the Quran (18:96).

translation: with u: a wood brought
from Aden by ship.
150.sharh: Qutr is the fragrant wood shipped in through Aden, the port where the aloeswood of India came ashore.

translation: When I saw his coquetry,
how he shunned me and put me off,
151.sharh: Al-Bahnasi's closing stanza returns to the beloved, his flirting, his coldness and his broken promises. This is the end of al-Bahnasi's poem; the rest is Ibn Zurayq's.

translation: out of my love for him I lamented
in Qutrub's triplets.
152.sharh: This is why he wrote the poem: the whole set of triplets is a lover's lament. Al-Zirikli used this closing line to show that the poem is not Qutrub's own, since it names him.

translation: And Ibn Zurayq set down in verse
a commentary on what has gone before,
153.sharh: Ibn Zurayq speaks of himself in the third person: he has put into verse a commentary on the stanzas above, explaining each vowel. This line is how the commentary's author is known.

translation: so that perhaps men of letters
will ask God's mercy for him.
154.sharh: He hopes that scholars of language who use the commentary will pray for God's mercy on him, a customary request at the end of a scholarly work.

translation: In it I have done my duty
in the service of al-Makhalibi,
155.sharh: He presents the commentary as a duty owed to his patron, Ahmad al-Makhalibi, as if written at his request or as a gift to him.

translation: Ahmad, the man of gifts
and of good stock.
156.sharh: He praises the patron for his generosity and his noble descent, as authors did for those they dedicated their work to.

translation: Whoever comes to him with hope
will have his hope of him;
157.sharh: No one who comes to Ahmad hoping for something goes away disappointed. Ibn Zurayq goes on praising his patron, as authors did when presenting their work.

translation: he makes happy all who reach him
among the learned in letters,
158.sharh: Scholars of language who reach him are made happy by his favour: he is a patron of learning, which is what Ibn Zurayq hopes he will be to him.

translation: whether by research he has carried out
or something new he has devised
159.sharh: Whatever the scholar brings him, research of his own or something new he has devised, is welcome, and Ibn Zurayq means himself and his own work.

translation: in explaining these triplets
in his polished verse.
160.sharh: The work in question is this commentary on the triplets, in carefully finished verse, which he offers to his patron as polished and free of faults.

translation: Praying and calling down peace
on the Prophet as often as
161.sharh: The commentary ends, as such works do, with blessings and peace on the Prophet, to last for ever.

translation: lightning flickers, or the white clouds
pour down their rain.
162.sharh: The blessing is to last as long as lightning flashes and the white clouds rain. The reciter repeats these last two lines to close.

1.1.2.head: مولَع
1.1.2.meaning: Given to, unable to leave off.

2.1.3.meaning: Has tormented; the same root gives tabarih, the pangs of love.

3.1.3.head: غَمر
3.1.3.meaning: Ghamr, with a: water deep enough to cover everything; here, his tears.

3.2.3.head: غِمر
3.2.3.meaning: Ghimr, with i: rancour kept hidden in the heart.

4.1.4.head: الغُمر
4.1.4.meaning: Ghumr, with u: a callow man, untried by experience.

5.1.1.head: الفَتح
5.1.1.meaning: Fath: the vowel a, written as a stroke above the letter; here, on the word's first letter.

5.2.1.head: الكَسر
5.2.1.meaning: Kasr: the vowel i, written as a stroke below the letter.

6.1.1.head: الضَّمّ
6.1.1.meaning: Damm: the vowel u, written as a small waw above the letter.

7.1.3.head: السَّلام
7.1.3.meaning: Salam, with a: the greeting of peace.

7.2.2.head: عَذول
7.2.2.meaning: My censurer, the man who blames me for loving.

8.1.3.head: السُّلام
8.1.3.meaning: Sulam, with u: the small bones of the fingers and the back of the hand.

10.2.4-5.meaning: The Prophet's saying: “Every sulama of a person owes charity”, reported by al-Bukhari.

12.1.1.head: صارَ
12.1.1.meaning: So I came to be (in). Al-Muhallabi's text and Cheikho's print have fa-sirtu, “so I travelled”.

12.1.4.meaning: Kulam, with u: hard, rugged ground.

15.1.3.meaning: Harra, with a: a lava field, ground of black, burnt-looking stones.

16.1.4.meaning: Hurra, with u: a free-born, noble woman.

19.1.3.head: حَلم
19.1.3.meaning: Halm, with a: the rotting of a hide, holed by grubs.

20.1.2.head: هَنَأَ
20.1.2.meaning: Has been sweet, has brought pleasure.

23.2.3.meaning: The one who gives sandals. Cheikho's print has muhdha, “shod in sibt sandals”.

23.2.4.head: السِّبت
23.2.4.meaning: Sibt, with i: tanned leather for sandals; al-Muhallabi glosses it as Yemeni sandals.

24.1.3.head: السُّبت
24.1.3.meaning: Subt, with u: a plant, which al-Muhallabi likens to marsh mallow.

25.2.1.head: كَسَرَ
25.2.1.meaning: Gave it an i, read it with kasra.

26.2.3.head: الرَّبرَب
26.2.3.meaning: Rabrab: a herd of wild cattle.

28.1.3.head: السُّهام
28.1.3.meaning: Suham, with u: the shimmer of the sun's rays in the heat; Ibn Zurayq makes it the light of the setting sun.

31.1.3.meaning: Da'wa, with a: a prayer, a call.

31.2.3.head: الدِّعوَة
31.2.3.meaning: Di'wa, with i: a claim to a lineage that is not one's own.

32.1.3.meaning: Du'wa, with u: a meal people are invited to.

32.2.4.head: رَجَب
32.2.4.meaning: Rajab: the seventh month of the Islamic year, one of the sacred months.

35.1.3.head: الشَّرب
35.1.3.meaning: Sharb, with a: a company of drinkers.

35.2.4.head: شِرب
35.2.4.meaning: Shirb, with i: one's share of water.

39.1.3.head: الخَرق
39.1.3.meaning: Kharq, with a: a wide, empty desert.

39.2.3.head: الخِرق
39.2.3.meaning: Khirq, with i: a generous young man who gives without stint.

44.2.2-3.meaning: “The rope of the bond”: the tie of love between two people.

48.1.4.head: القُسط
48.1.4.meaning: Qust, with u: costus, a fragrant Indian root burned as incense and used as medicine.

51.1.3.head: العَرف
51.1.3.meaning: Arf, with a: a sweet smell.

52.1.2.head: العُرف
52.1.2.meaning: Urf, with u: what is right and good.

55.1.3.meaning: Lamma, with a: a touch of madness.

55.2.4.meaning: Limma, with i: hair worn long, below the ears.

56.1.4.meaning: Lumma, with u: companions, a band of friends.

60.1.3.head: مُسك
60.1.3.meaning: Musk, with u: what keeps a person alive, food and drink; Ibn Zurayq glosses it as tight-fistedness.

63.1.1.head: مَلَأَ
63.1.1.meaning: Have filled. Al-Muhallabi's text and Cheikho's print have ballat, “have wet”.

63.1.3.head: حَجر
63.1.3.meaning: Hajr, with a: the lap, the front of the garment.

64.1.3-4.meaning: Ibn Hujr, with u: Imru' al-Qays, the pre-Islamic poet, whose father Hujr ibn al-Harith of Kinda ruled the tribe of Asad.

67.2.4.head: السِّقط
67.2.4.meaning: Siqt, with i: the spark struck from a fire-stick, as Ibn Zurayq explains it.

68.1.3.head: السُّقط
68.1.3.meaning: Suqt, with u: in al-Muhallabi's commentary, sparks falling from a fire-stick; Ibn Zurayq makes it a child born before its term. Ibn Malik allows all three vowels in all three senses.

69.2.4.head: زَند
69.2.4.meaning: Zand: a fire-stick, the wood that is struck to make fire.

71.1.3.head: صَرَّة
71.1.3.meaning: Sarra, with a: a crowd, a clamour.

72.1.4.head: صُرَّة
72.1.4.meaning: Surra, with u: a purse, a knotted cloth for coins.

72.2.1.head: خَردَلَة
72.2.1.meaning: A mustard seed, a byword for the tiniest amount.

79.1.3.head: الجَدّ
79.1.3.meaning: Jadd, with a: grandfather; also fortune, greatness.

80.2.1.head: المُعَطَّل
80.2.1.meaning: Disused, like the abandoned well of the Quran (22:45).

83.1.3.head: الجَواري
83.1.3.meaning: Jawar, with a: girls, slave girls; also ships.

84.1.3.head: الجُؤار
84.1.3.meaning: Juwar, with u: a loud cry; the hamza of ju'ar is softened.

87.1.3.head: عَمَرَ
87.1.3.meaning: Amarat, with a: became lived in again.

87.2.3.head: عَمِرَ
87.2.3.meaning: Amirat, with i: lived long; Ibn Zurayq glosses it as becoming rich.

88.1.3.head: عَمُرَ
88.1.3.meaning: Amurat, with u: flourished, was brought under cultivation.

88.2.3.head: رَسم
88.2.3.meaning: Rasm: the trace left of an abandoned dwelling.

89.2.1.head: كَسر
89.2.1.meaning: Its i: the vowel of the middle letter here.

92.1.5.meaning: Humam, with u: a man's name.

95.1.4.meaning: Mala, with a: a crowd of people; al-Muhallabi makes it open desert.

95.2.3.head: مِلء
95.2.3.meaning: Mil', with i: the fill of a vessel; here, brimful.

96.1.3.head: المُلاء
96.1.3.meaning: Mula', with u: fine wraps, sheets of cloth.

96.2.2-3.meaning: “O for the wonder”: an exclamation of amazement.

98.1.3.head: العَبقَرِيّ
98.1.3.meaning: Abqari: richly worked cloth, named for Abqar, a place the Arabs believed belonged to the jinn.

99.1.2.head: الشَّكل
99.1.2.meaning: Shakl, with a: likeness, a match.

99.2.2.head: الشِّكل
99.2.2.meaning: Shikl, with i: coquetry, flirtatious charm.

100.1.2.head: الشُّكل
100.1.2.meaning: Shukl, with u: hobbles, ropes that tie an animal's legs.

100.2.3.meaning: “Ah, my ruin”: a cry of lament.

103.1.3.meaning: Raqaq, with a: soft, sandy ground.

103.2.4.meaning: Riqaq, with i: flats the water has drained from; Ibn Zurayq makes it bread.

104.1.1-2.meaning: “Did they speak”. Cheikho's print has “did they not speak”.

104.1.4.meaning: Ruqaq, with u: thin flatbread; Ibn Zurayq makes it a kind of land.

106.2.3.head: النُّصُب
106.2.3.meaning: Nusub: stones set up as markers.

107.1.2.head: القَمَّة
107.1.2.meaning: Qamma, with a: what a lion takes in its jaws.

107.2.4.meaning: Qimma, with i: a peak, the top of the head.

111.1.3.head: الصَّلّ
111.1.3.meaning: Sall, with a: the clang of iron, in Ibn Zurayq's gloss.

111.2.3.head: الصِّلّ
111.2.3.meaning: Sill, with i: a deadly snake.

112.1.3.head: الصُّلّ
112.1.3.meaning: Sull, with u: food or water gone bad, in Ibn Zurayq's gloss.

112.2.3.meaning: A man sitting with his knees drawn up and bound to his back by his cloak.

118.2.3-4.meaning: “The gazelle's neck”: a byword for a long, beautiful neck.

119.1.3.meaning: Laqa, with a: something thrown aside as worthless.

120.1.3.meaning: Luqa, with u: honey boiled until it sets, in Ibn Zurayq's gloss.

123.1.3.head: رَشَأ
123.1.3.meaning: Rasha', with a: a young gazelle.

123.2.3.head: الرِّشاء
123.2.3.meaning: Risha', with i: a well rope.

127.1.3.head: الزَّجاج
127.1.3.meaning: Zajaj, with a: cloves, in Ibn Zurayq's gloss; Ibn Malik gives all three vowels for glass.

127.2.3.meaning: Zijaj, with i: the iron points at the foot of spears.

128.2.1.head: وادي
128.2.1.meaning: Wadin, “a valley”: so the reciter says, as his text has it; perhaps for wuddun, “a love”, which makes better sense of the comparison with glass.

129.2.2.head: زَجّ
129.2.2.meaning: Zajj: thrusting with a spear, as the reciter says it. The iron spike at the butt of a spear is zujj, plural zijaj.

131.1.3.meaning: Manna, with a: a snake, in Ibn Zurayq's gloss.

131.2.3.meaning: Minna, with i: a favour its giver keeps bringing up.

135.2.3.meaning: Imma, with i: good fortune, ease and plenty.

136.1.3.meaning: Umma, with u: a people, a community.

139.2.3.head: القِرى
139.2.3.meaning: Qira, with i: the food of hospitality, what is set before a guest.

142.2.1.head: مَكَّة
142.2.1.meaning: Mecca. The name takes a tanwin here for the metre, which it does not take in prose.

142.2.3.head: يَثرِب
142.2.3.meaning: Yathrib: the old name of Medina.

143.1.4.head: الظَّلم
143.1.4.meaning: Zalm, with a: the sheen and moisture of the teeth.

143.2.3.head: الظِّلم
143.2.3.meaning: Zilm, with i: the male ostrich, in Ibn Zurayq's gloss.

147.2.1.head: القِطر
147.2.1.meaning: Qitr, with i: molten brass, as in the Quran (18:96).

148.1.1.head: القُطر
148.1.1.meaning: Qutr, with u: aloeswood, burned as incense.

148.1.2-3.meaning: “The water of his nose”: his breath.

150.2.2.head: عَدَن
150.2.2.meaning: Aden: the port in south Yemen where ships from India brought perfumes.

151.2.2.head: مَطل
151.2.2.meaning: Putting off, delaying what is promised.

152.1.1.head: رَثى
152.1.1.meaning: I lamented. Al-Muhallabi's text and Cheikho's print have “I composed, describing him”.

152.2.2.head: قُطرُب
152.2.2.meaning: Qutrub: Abu Ali Muhammad ibn al-Mustanir, the Basran grammarian and pupil of Sibawayh, d. 206 AH (821 CE), the first to write a book of such triplets. Sibawayh nicknamed him after a little creature that never stops scurrying, because he found him at his door before dawn.

153.1.1-2.head: ابن زُرَيق
153.1.1-2.meaning: Ibn Zurayq: Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Zurayq, author of the verse commentary, not the Baghdadi poet of the same name. Sezgin dates his death to 977 AH (1569 CE); another catalogue gives 803 AH.

154.2.2-3.meaning: Men of letters, scholars of Arabic.

155.2.3.meaning: Al-Makhalibi: Ahmad al-Makhalibi, a patron of whom nothing else is known.

156.1.1.head: أَحمَد
156.1.1.meaning: Ahmad: Ahmad al-Makhalibi, Ibn Zurayq's patron, named in the line before.

161.1.1-2.meaning: Calling down God's blessing and peace on the Prophet.
